sources.population: Shh-Light2/NIH-3T3 reporter cells, pathway-mutant cells and mouse tumor allografts

questions.title: Hedgehog signaling and Smoothened
questions.text: Hedgehog signaling can sustain the growth of some tumors. In cell experiments, itraconazole reduced pathway activity and prevented Smoothened from accumulating in the primary cilium, a signaling compartment on the cell surface. Pathway-mapping experiments placed its action near Smoothened, although this study did not directly establish a binding site. Fluconazole did not share the Hedgehog effect under the tested conditions.

questions.title: Cholesterol transport and blood-vessel growth
questions.text: In endothelial-cell experiments, itraconazole caused cholesterol transport inhibition. Cholesterol became trapped in endolysosomes while mTOR signaling and proliferation fell; supplying cholesterol to the cell membrane partly reversed these effects. Later binding and competition experiments identified the cholesterol-transport protein NPC1 as a target, alongside a separate VDAC1–AMPK pathway. These mechanisms help explain the anti-angiogenesis rationale, but do not establish cancer benefit in patients.

questions.title: Microtubules, cell division and apoptosis
questions.text: In lung-cancer models, fenbendazole partly disrupted microtubules, arrested cell division and increased apoptosis. Experiments also found altered p53 activity and glucose handling. The results support several possible contributors to cancer-cell injury. Cell cultures and mouse xenografts do not establish an effective or safe anticancer exposure in people.

questions.title: Hyphal growth and invasiveness
questions.text: Fluconazole inhibited the yeast-to-hypha transition in susceptible Candida albicans isolates when present during both growth and hyphal induction. Resistant isolates could still form hyphae. This is evidence about fungal morphology under laboratory conditions. It does not by itself show that tissue invasion is prevented in patients.

questions.title: Biofilms and resistance
questions.text: Fluconazole should not be described as a general biofilm-destroying drug. In experiments with clinical Candida albicans isolates, maturing biofilms became less susceptible, with changes in efflux-pump and drug-target gene expression. Preventing early biofilm development and removing an established biofilm are different questions; susceptibility of free-floating yeast does not settle either one.

questions.title: Why fluconazole and itraconazole differ
questions.text: Shared antifungal action does not mean identical repurposing mechanisms. In the original Hedgehog screening experiments, itraconazole suppressed the pathway while fluconazole showed no detectable inhibition at the tested concentrations.

questions.title: Testing the autophagy explanation
questions.text: The Parkinson disease experiments went beyond measuring autophagy markers: blocking AMPK or autophagy weakened metformin-associated protection in toxin-injured cells. Mitochondrial damage and oxidative-stress measurements changed as well. That supports a causal contribution in this model, with limits from inhibitor specificity and the experimental exposure. It does not establish that the same process improves Parkinson disease in people.

questions.title: Testing the WNT–TCF explanation
questions.text: In colorectal-cancer experiments, forcing TCF signaling back on rescued cells from some low-concentration ivermectin effects. Ivermectin also inhibited TCF-dependent mouse xenografts but not a TCF-independent comparison model. This is stronger mechanistic evidence than an association between a pathway marker and cell death. Its relevance still depends on tumor biology, exposure and formulation; it does not establish clinical cancer benefit.

questions.title: mTOR and autophagy
questions.text: Rapamycin-sensitive mTOR signaling regulates the ULK–Atg13–FIP200 machinery that helps initiate autophagy. In cell experiments, rapamycin increased autophagic flux, and disrupting ULK or Atg13 weakened that response. This explains a cellular recycling mechanism; whether changing it helps a particular disease requires separate evidence.

questions.title: Inflammation and periodontal bone
questions.text: In aged mice, rapamycin-associated periodontal bone recovery accompanied a lower RANKL/OPG ratio, fewer bone-resorbing osteoclast markers and altered inflammatory signaling. The study did not establish that autophagy caused the bone improvement, and mouse tissue findings do not establish human periodontal benefit.

questions.title: Blood flow and tissue oxygenation
questions.text: Preserving cGMP supplies a rationale for studying vascular function, but vasodilation, blood-flow velocity and tissue oxygenation are different measurements. A controlled sildenafil experiment in healthy men exposed to low oxygen measured these separately. Some measures of cerebral vascular regulation improved, while the reported cortical oxygenation measures did not show a significant drug effect. This does not support a general claim that sildenafil increases local oxygenation in every condition.

questions.title: Cerebral perfusion and oxygenation
questions.text: A small tadalafil trial after small-vessel stroke found a modest increase in cortical oxygen saturation at three hours. That near-infrared signal was a surrogate for local perfusion, with no significant overall change in the Doppler blood-velocity measure. PASTIS then measured brain perfusion directly with MRI and found no significant increase in the prespecified subcortical measures after a single dose. These studies test a vascular rationale; they do not establish improved cognition or prevention of another stroke.
